sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Dumbbell Hip Thrust is a glute-dominant exercise performed with your upper back supported on a bench and a dumbbell placed across the hips for resistance.

This movement targets the glutes through a full range of hip extension and is one of the most effective exercises for building glute strength and size.

Using a dumbbell makes this variation easy to set up and accessible for all fitness levels, while still providing meaningful resistance for glute development.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- High glute activation throughout the full range of motion
- Easy to set up compared to barbell hip thrusts
- Reduced stress on the lower back
- Builds hip extension strength for improved athletic performance
- Improves lockout strength in squats and deadlifts
- Accessible for beginners and advanced lifters alike
- Helps correct quad-dominant movement patterns

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Glutes (Gluteus Maximus)

Secondary: Hamstrings, Quadriceps, Hip Adductors, Core, Erector Spinae

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Sit on the ground with your back against a bench, positioned at around shoulder blade height.
2. Hold a dumbbell on your hips securely with both hands.
3. Place your feet flat on the ground, roughly shoulder-width apart.
4. Bend your knees at approximately a 90-degree angle.
5. Keep your chin slightly tucked and your gaze forward.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the ground.
2. Push your hips upward until your thighs are parallel to the floor.
3. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top of the movement.
4. Maintain a neutral spine throughout — avoid hyperextending your lower back.
5. Slowly lower your hips back down to the starting position with control.
6. Repeat the movement for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Hyperextending the lower back at the top of the movement
- Pushing through the toes instead of the heels
- Allowing the knees to cave inward during the thrust
- Positioning too far forward or back on the bench
- Not achieving full hip extension at the top
- Rushing through reps without controlling the descent
- Letting the dumbbell shift or roll off the hips

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Dumbbell (appropriate weight for your level)
- Sturdy Flat Bench or Box
- Optional: Hip Pad or Towel (for comfort on hips)
- Flat, Non-Slip Floor Surface

sections.heading: Bench Setup
sections.content:
1. Position a sturdy bench against a wall or rack so it doesn't slide.
2. The bench height should allow your shoulder blades to rest on the edge.
3. Ensure the bench is stable and won't tip during the movement.
4. If using a box, make sure it is heavy enough to stay in place.
5. A standard flat bench height works well for most people.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Shoulder-width apart, flat on the floor.
2. Shins: Approximately vertical at the top of the movement.
3. Back: Shoulder blades resting on the edge of the bench.
4. Dumbbell: Centered on the hips, held securely with both hands.
5. Head: Neutral position, chin slightly tucked.
6. Core: Braced throughout the entire movement.
7. Knees: Tracking in line with toes, bent at roughly 90 degrees.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Hip Thrust: Heavier loading potential with a barbell
- Kettlebell Hip Thrust: Alternative loading with a kettlebell
- Glute Bridge: Floor-based version without bench elevation
- Single Leg Hip Thrust: Unilateral variation for balance correction
- Banded Hip Thrust: Resistance band variation for constant tension
- Cable Pull-Through: Standing hip hinge with cable resistance

sections.heading: Hip Thrust Variations
sections.content:
Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Standard bench-supported thrust with dumbbell
Single Leg Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Unilateral version for imbalance correction
Paused Hip Thrust: Hold at top for increased time under tension
Banded Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Added band resistance at lockout
Foot-Elevated Hip Thrust: Feet raised to increase range of motion
Tempo Hip Thrust: Slow eccentric for enhanced muscle building

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
No Bench Available: Perform glute bridges from the floor
Knee Discomfort: Adjust foot position wider or narrower
Lower Back Pain: Focus on core bracing and avoid hyperextension
Hip Discomfort: Use a pad or towel under the dumbbell
No Dumbbell: Use a kettlebell, plate, or resistance band
Limited Mobility: Start with bodyweight hip thrusts to build range
